                                                Dear Dr. Chadwell:                                                                                  •

                                           In pursuance of our telephone conversation of the other
                                   • day, and in accordance with your request, I am confirming ln
                                     writing the results ·1 transmitted to ·you over the phone.
                                             ' It is well known that in theodolite observations, elevations
                            •       can- ~e- genera!1y- obta1ned more accurately than the azimuths since
            •                       the :rormer depend only· on- accurate leveling but the- latter depend.
                                    upon a determination or the true north. Since most theodolite·
                                    observers are interested in relative rates and not in absolute
                                    positions, it is no surprise that they do not pay too much atten-
                                    tion to the exact determination of their zero points. Further,
                                    it is quite easy for even an observer of some experience to make
                                    an e~ror 1n reading of some multiple of whole degrees. The
                                    observation made at Limestone, therefore 1 can very well be assumed
                                    to. have both a zero point error  .  and an incorrect scale reading.
                                                        •

                                               At the mean time ot observation, calculations made at the
                                    observatory here show that Jupiter had, at Presque Isle, an
                                    azimuth of 163° and an elevation or 58.5°. This alone is f.. sur-
                                    fi~.~ent.ly_~J..9~e. to the mean or the readings from two stations to
                                    serve as· strong evidence that the object observed was Jupiter.
                .;'\
                                    However, the clinching a~ument comes when one compares Jupiter's
                 -                  !:~~~ .. Pf..motion in elevation and azimuth during the observation .
                                    and -the rates noted on the theodolitej at Presque Isle. The com-
                                    puted increment in elevation was 0.2 degrees (as compared to the
    •                               observed 0.3 degrees) and the corresponding increment in azimuth
-                                   was 1.8 degrees (as against the observed .1.9 degrees): In view
                                  . of -this strikingly close agreement ~n rates as well as general .
                                    position in the sky, it would be an outrage to probability theory
                                    to ,consider that the object observed was anything other. than th~
                                    time-honored planet Jupiter. The _prosecut1on rests its case! · .
